title: Federal prosecutors stumble in case over Ontario nuclear plant's worst fish kill

image.caption: A gizzard shad is held above a fishing net by a provincial conservation worker. The temperature-sensitive species is at the centre of a massive fish kill at Ontario's Bruce Nuclear generating station in 2025. (Upper Thames Conservation Authority)

blocks.text: Crown prosecutors have withdrawn and re-laid charges over a massive fish kill in 2025 against Bruce Power, the private operator of Canada's largest nuclear plant, after initially filing the case in the wrong court.
Bruce Power is due back in court Dec. 9 after the Crown withdrew original 2 charges

Crown prosecutors were forced to start over in their case against the operator of Canada's largest nuclear power plant after initially filing federal Fisheries Act charges in the wrong court over a massive 2025 fish kill.

Bruce Power was charged under Canada's Fisheries Act in October with unlawfully killing fish and violating the conditions of its federal fisheries authorization in connection with a massive fish kill at the plant in 2025.
The case came before a provincial offences court in Walkerton, Ont., on Tuesday, where Crown prosecutors withdrew the charges so they could be brought before the proper court.
The Walkerton court office told CBC News that the new charges are identical to those withdrawn on Tuesday. Bruce Power is now scheduled to appear in criminal court on Dec. 9.
The Public Prosecution Service of Canada, the federal agency responsible for prosecuting offences under federal law, including the Fisheries Act, was unable to immediately comment on Wednesday.
Megan Adams, Bruce Power's director of corporate communications and marketing, declined to comment on the court mix-up, citing the ongoing legal proceedings.
A fish kill of unprecedented scale
Millions of gizzard shad were killed after they overwhelmed the plant's cooling water system in February 2025, forcing Bruce Power to shutdown one reactor and reduce power at another.

As many as 4.95 million gizzard shad died in the incident, with dead fish washing ashore in lakeside communities for days. At the plant, the fish had to be scooped out with a crane and hauled to a landfill.
Dead gizzard shad seen here on a beach on Lake Huron in the spring of 2025 were reported washing up in many localities along the coast. (Submitted by Saugeen Ojibway Nation)

Federal and provincial records obtained by CBC News also revealed the incident "challenged reactor safety" and raised concerns about the growing risks posed by climate change to nuclear power plant cooling systems.
It was the largest fish kill in the plant's history and prompted an investigation by Fisheries and Oceans Canada, culminating in the two federal charges.

Bruce Power has operated the sprawling nuclear generating facility on the shores of Lake Huron, about 200 kilometres northwest of Toronto, since 2001, when it took over operations from provincially owned Ontario Power Generation.
The eight-reactor facility, originally built by Ontario Hydro in the 1970s and '80s, supplies roughly 30 per cent of Ontario's electricity.
